newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian forces break up Kashmir poll protests.
newsitem.headline: Indian forces break up Kashmir poll protests.

text.p: Indian security forces fired tear gas shells and shot bullets into the air on Friday in Srinagar, summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, to disperse anti-election demonstrators, witnesses said.
The protests were against the state's first local elections, due to begin on Saturday, since a separatist rebellion erupted in the Himalayan region six years ago.
Tens of thousands of soldiers, paramilitary troopers and police officers fanned out across the state amid concerns for the safety of candidates and voters.
About 200 people shouting anti-election slogans took to the streets of Srinagar after Moslem Friday prayers at the main mosque, the witnesses said.
Paramilitary troops fired shots in the air and charged the protesters after they began throwing stones, they said.
The demonstrators dispersed and there were no reports of injuries.
Police fired tear gas shells earlier to disperse a smaller protest against the poll. Again, there were no reports of injuries.
Most businesses and shops were closed in Srinagar on Friday at the start of a 48-hour protest strike called by separatists.

Jammu and Kashmir is mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state. Militant groups in Kashmir have been fighting either for independence or merger with neighbouring Pakistan, which rules one-third of the Kashmir region and claims the rest.
Two separatist leaders were taken to hospital with injuries they said they suffered when beaten by soldiers.

Yasin Malik, president of the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, and Jawed Mir, vice president, told Reuters from their hospital beds that a group of soldiers entered the home of a friend they were visiting in Baramulla, 60 km (35 miles) from Srinagar, on Friday morning.
They said the soldiers beat them with rifle butts and pistols before putting them in a taxi for Srinagar.

Reshi Showkat, house surgeon at the Hospital for Bone and Joint Surgery in Srinagar, said they suffered multiple bruises on their arms and legs, and that Mir had been cut on the left ear. He said he was awaiting the results of X-rays.
Army spokesman Major P. Purushottam said Malik and Mir had been leading demonstrators who approached army officers while they were defusing a crude bomb.
The soldiers were forced to prevent the protesters from advancing and put Malik and Mir in a taxi for Srinagar, he said.
Asked about claims they had been beaten, the spokesman said: "I don't think there is much credence to their story."
About 200,000 security officers were on duty for Saturday's first round of polling in 26 of 87 constituencies in the state, which has about eight million people.
Polls were due to open at 0130 GMT.
Other areas were to vote on September 16, 21 and 30 to let polling officers and security forces move between districts.

The election is viewed as a test of Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's strategy for restoring democratic rule to a region where more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence in six years.
On Friday, London-based Amnesty International expressed concern at the lack of election observers and said that human rights abuses "could reach a new peak" during the election.
